title: God, divine designations, and titles
original_terms: Hebrew אֵל (El), אֱלֹהִים (elohim), אֱלוֹהַּ (eloah); Aramaic אֱלָהּ (elah); Greek θεός (theos). Separate title records: El Shaddai, El Elyon, Ancient of Days / Aramaic עַתִּיק יוֹמִין (attiq yomin).
default_explanation: A plural form alone does not prove the Trinity, and a shared designation does not give every referent equal identity or status.
translation_key: Identify the referent through grammar, narrative, and contrast. Preserve separate title explanations instead of reducing all titles to a single proposed etymology.
initial_orientation: Genesis 1 identifies the Creator. Genesis 14 uses El Elyon in Melchizedek's blessing. Genesis 17 uses El Shaddai in a covenant setting. Daniel 7 presents the Ancient of Days in a vision. First Corinthians 8 distinguishes other claims to deity from its confession.
core_study:
#### Local reading

El, elohim, eloah, Aramaic elah, and Greek theos are distinct lexical records used in divine designations. Their reference depends on the clause and setting. Elohim has a plural form but often takes singular syntax when referring to Israel's God. Its morphology alone is therefore not proof of a plurality of persons within God. Nor does the word's application to other figures automatically make those figures equal to Yahweh.

Genesis 1:1 names God as the agent of creation. Genesis 14:18–22 includes El Elyon, the Most High, and identifies Abram's allegiance in the narrative. Genesis 17:1 uses El Shaddai in a covenant scene. “God Almighty” is an established rendering of Shaddai, but proposed derivations involving sufficiency, mountains, or other historical associations should not be asserted as settled lexical facts. A translation can preserve the title and footnote uncertainty where its derivation matters.

Daniel 7:9–14 uses Aramaic, not Hebrew, for the Ancient of Days and the human-like figure before him. Attiq concerns being aged or advanced; the visionary title and its setting communicate authority and judgment. Psalm 82 and Exodus 7:1 complicate simplistic assertions that a divine designation has only one possible type of referent. They require local analysis rather than a list of English “God” occurrences treated as interchangeable evidence.

#### Translation and default explanation

Translate God, god, divine beings, or another warranted description according to the actual referent and syntax. Modern capitalization expresses interpretation; it is not independent ancient manuscript evidence. Keep El Shaddai, El Elyon, and Ancient of Days as title records linked to their component lemmas, without flattening the titles into generic synonyms.

The default explanation is that a designation's semantic range and a passage's assertion about its bearer are different questions. Calling someone elohim in a commissioned or judicial setting does not automatically identify that person as the Creator. Calling the Father God does not by itself settle every statement about the Son; the particular relations and predicates must also be read.

#### Biblical and canonical development

First Corinthians 8:4–6 places the confession of one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, in an argument about idols and allegiance. The parallel claims about all things being from the Father and through Jesus are central to its interpretation. Read those clauses together before importing a theological framework into either title.

The useful trajectory concerns the Creator's uniqueness, competing divine claims, and the New Testament's account of God and Christ. The working synthesis should show how exclusive worship and the passage's distinctions coexist. A theology review asks what identity, agency, relation, and worship each text actually attributes. Neither a plural ending nor a capitalization convention can substitute for that argument. Historical lexicon categories are useful lookup aids but should not be treated as a final resolution of contested divine-council or Christological passages.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: divine designations

This is a **multi-language designations hub**, not one lemma: Hebrew **אֵל (*’el*)**, **אֱלֹהִים (*’elohim*)**, **אֱלוֹהַּ (*’eloah*)**; Aramaic **אֱלָהּ (*’elah*)**; Greek **θεός (*theos*)**; plus separate titles such as **El Elyon**, **El Shaddai**, and Aramaic **Ancient of Days**. Each expression must be read by morphology, modifier, referent and literary genre. *Elohim* has morphologically plural form but can take singular agreement referring to Israel's God; the form alone proves neither a plurality of persons nor a single ontology for every spiritual referent.

**Reference changes by setting.** In Gen 1:1 *elohim* refers to the sole Creator of the narrated world. Gen 14:18–22 uses **El Elyon** in Melchizedek's blessing, identified in Abraham's response with Yahweh; Gen 17:1 uses **El Shaddai** in covenantal speech. The historical derivation of *Shaddai* is debated and must not be forced into a “mountain,” “breast,” or “Almighty” etymology without source evidence. In Dan 7:9 the **Ancient of Days** is a literary visionary title; age imagery does not assert that Yahweh is an elderly physical being. 1 Cor 8:4–6 acknowledges broader claims to gods/lords while confessing one God and one Lord.

**Theological layer.** A biblical description of God's unique identity requires the predicates and plot of these passages rather than assigning all distinct titles one flat dictionary meaning. Category-based use of “elohim” for spiritual beings can be considered from contextual occurrences, without treating every referent as equal to Yahweh. **Limit:** selected records do not constitute a universal concordance of *elohim*, nor a settled etymology of all divine epithets.
theology_check: Distinguish lexical designation, unique divine identity, and the canon's developed confession.

title: Lord, master, hosts, sovereignty
original_terms: Hebrew אָדוֹן (adon), אֲדֹנָי (Adonai); Greek κύριος (kyrios). Linked titles: Yahweh Sabaoth / Yahweh of hosts; παντοκράτωρ (pantokratōr).
default_explanation: Kyrios does not always mean the divine name. Conversely, its use in a divine-name quotation should not be flattened to polite human address.
translation_key: Choose Lord, lord, master, or an explanatory title from the actual referent. Explain capitalization as an editorial choice rather than an original Greek distinction.
initial_orientation: Genesis 24:18 contains a human address as lord. First Samuel 1:3 uses Yahweh of hosts. Psalm 110 distinguishes Yahweh and my lord. Philippians 2 places the confession of Jesus as Lord within exaltation and scriptural language.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Lord and master vocabulary can name ownership, authority, respectful address, or divine sovereignty. In Genesis 24:18, the polite address to Abraham's servant does not identify him as Yahweh. Adon and related forms therefore need their actual referents. Adonai functions prominently in address to God, while a source record must still distinguish it from the divine name and from other inflected lord forms.

Psalm 110:1 is a particularly important case: Yahweh speaks to “my lord.” Rendering both simply as Lord can hide the two Hebrew expressions and the relation between speaker and addressee. Matthew 22:41–46 uses the psalm in a question about the Messiah's relationship to David. The force of the argument depends on more than the dictionary range of lord; it depends on whose lord is being described and on the scriptural scene.

Yahweh of hosts combines the divine name with army or host vocabulary. First Samuel 1:3 places this title in a worship setting. Context must determine the relevance of earthly armies, heavenly hosts, or comprehensive sovereignty; the word “hosts” does not automatically specify one particular angelic hierarchy. Pantokratōr contributes a Greek expression of sovereign power, notably in Revelation, but it should retain its own record rather than be treated as a mechanically identical translation of every Hebrew title.

#### Translation and default explanation

Use Lord, master, or sir where the actual relationship warrants it. Retain Yahweh for the Hebrew divine name under the project convention. In interlinear presentation, identify both words in Psalm 110:1 rather than producing two unexplained “Lord” rows. Explain “Yahweh of hosts” on first use without substituting an unverified full theological paraphrase into the text.

The default explanation is that kyrios can be an ordinary title or carry the significance of a divine-name quotation. The word alone does not decide which. A New Testament citation of a Yahweh passage applied to Jesus needs its source and reception identified; a polite vocative in dialogue should not receive that same explanation merely because its spelling matches.

#### Biblical and canonical development

Philippians 2:9–11 applies Isaiah 45:22–23's universal homage language to the confession of Jesus as Lord. Romans 10:9–13 similarly connects confession, invocation, and scriptural promise. These are useful bounded trajectories for divine-name Christology, and they provide stronger evidence than an unsorted concordance of kyrios.

The working synthesis explains Jesus' exalted authority in the text's relation to God's sovereignty while preserving its statements about the Father and the Son. Review whether a proposed translation has either flattened a significant quotation into ordinary social address or inflated a routine address into a divine-identity claim. The same caution applies to human lordship: its presence describes authority without necessarily approving every exercise of that authority.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: lordship and masters

Hebrew **אָדוֹן (*’adon*)** can identify a human superior or master; **אֲדֹנָי (*’adonay*)** is a divine form of address in relevant contexts. Greek **κύριος (*kyrios*)** can address a human lord/master, function as a respectful title, or denote God or Jesus; actual referent decides, not the mere presence of the word. **Yahweh of hosts** describes divine lordship by a separate Hebrew name-plus-title construction. Greek **παντοκράτωρ (*pantokratōr*)**, commonly “almighty/all-sovereign,” is distinct from kyrios and from a generic human “master.”

**Actors and texts.** In Gen 24:18 the addressee called lord is a human participant; inferring divine status from the gloss would be absurd. 1 Sam 1:3 speaks of Yahweh of hosts in a worship setting, invoking God's rule over hosts without deciding from this one clause precisely which “hosts” are being pictured. Ps 110:1 differentiates Yahweh and the speaker's “my lord”; a contextual royal figure and later messianic reception are distinct analytic stages. Phil 2:9–11 confesses Jesus as **Lord** within exaltation and scriptural echoes: its theological force derives from Isaiah's worship language and the argument, not simply because *kyrios* is inherently divine.

**Rendering rules.** Keep proper name Yahweh distinct from the Hebrew title Adonai and Greek kyrios. Later manuscript practices or translation conventions that use “LORD” to represent YHWH must not be mistaken for evidence that the Hebrew original wrote *’adon*. **Limit:** broad *kyrios* social address and Septuagint substitution patterns require occurrence-specific control and cannot be decided through English capitalization.
theology_check: Assess authority, kingship, and divine-name reception through context and identifiable scriptural connections.

title: One, alone, I am he
original_terms: Hebrew אֶחָד (echad), אֲנִי הוּא (ani hu); Greek εἷς (heis), ἐγώ εἰμι (egō eimi). A numeral and an identity formula require different records.
default_explanation: Echad is not a technical compound-unity word. The words I am do not by themselves establish a divine claim in every occurrence.
translation_key: Explain syntactic possibilities for the Shema before choosing one/alone in translation. Identify an ordinary self-identification separately from a proposed scriptural echo.
initial_orientation: Deuteronomy 6:4 belongs to Israel's summons to exclusive love and loyalty. Isaiah 43:10 concerns Yahweh's identity and witnesses. John 8:58 places Jesus' statement in an argument involving Abraham.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Echad is an ordinary Hebrew word for one. Its use can concern one item, a unified group, an exclusive referent, or another contextual construction. It is not a technical theological word meaning “compound unity.” A numeral used of a joined pair or collective does not carry that collective meaning in every occurrence. The composition of what is called one must be established from the subject and clause.

Deuteronomy 6:4–5 places the confession about Yahweh within the summons to love him wholly. Renderings emphasizing “Yahweh is one” or “Yahweh alone” reflect questions about the Hebrew clause and its covenant setting. The practical emphasis on exclusive allegiance is strong; explaining the clause as a mathematical proof for a later theological system overstates the lexical evidence. The following command should remain part of the unit being studied.

Ani hu and egō eimi are identity expressions, not equivalent records for echad. Isaiah 43:10 uses God's self-identification within a proclamation of his uniqueness. John 8:58 uses egō eimi in a striking contrast with Abraham's coming into existence. Its temporal construction and the Gospel's presentation of Jesus matter. John 9:9, however, places the same Greek expression on the formerly blind man's lips as ordinary self-identification. This is a direct check against making every “I am” occurrence a divine claim. John 11:25 explicitly supplies the predicate “the resurrection and the life”; grammatically it is not an absolute, predicate-less I-am saying. Its theological significance should be argued from what Jesus claims in that setting.

#### Translation and default explanation

Preserve one, alone, or the appropriate identity expression with a note where the alternatives materially affect interpretation. Do not translate echad as “a compound unity” or egō eimi as “I am Yahweh” merely to make a theological reading explicit. Explanatory conclusions belong in the commentary, supported by the actual wording and its scriptural connections.

The default explanation is that the words can contribute to a theological argument without independently encoding its whole conclusion. John 10:30's statement about Father and Son being one needs the surrounding claims and grammar; its neuter one does not simply mean that they are one person. First Corinthians 8:4–6 likewise requires its parallel clauses and argument about idols.

#### Biblical and canonical development

A focused trajectory connects Israel's confession of exclusive allegiance with New Testament monotheistic and Christological claims. A separate identity-formula trajectory may connect Isaiah's divine self-identification with relevant Johannine uses. Classify the connection as a possible allusion or interpretive reception unless the passage explicitly cites it; lexical overlap alone is not enough.

The working synthesis should state what the selected texts affirm about God's uniqueness and Jesus' relation to God, then identify the inferential steps. James 2:19 shows that confessing one God is not, by itself, the complete response the letter seeks. Theology review should preserve that ethical context. Neither a “compound unity” gloss nor an automatic dismissal of every Johannine identity formula provides an adequate reading.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: numerical one and divine identity speech

Hebrew **אֶחָד (*’eḥad*)** and Greek **εἷς (*heis*)** are number/oneness vocabulary; Hebrew **אֲנִי הוּא (*’ani hu’*)** and Greek **ἐγώ εἰμι (*egō eimi*)** are personal identity expressions, not another way of spelling the numeral. The first may count, classify or assert unity/exclusivity in context; the second may identify a speaker ordinarily, or carry special revelatory resonance where quoted scriptural echoes establish it. Neither *’eḥad* nor an unqualified “I am” means “Trinity,” “compound unity,” or the divine name by definition.

**Critical contexts.** Deut 6:4 speaks of Yahweh, Israel's God, as one/alone within a summons to exclusive allegiance in 6:5–9; alternative translations of the Shema require syntactic analysis rather than an argument from a supposed inherent “compound” meaning of *’eḥad*. Isa 43:10 uses Yahweh's **“I am He”** speech in an anti-idolatry witness argument, emphasizing identity and uniqueness. John 8:58 places Jesus' **“I am”** statement into a claim concerning Abraham's time, not a routine reply to “who is there?” Its unusual temporal contrast and ensuing response may support a stronger identity claim, but the grammatical phrase alone is not a divine name.

**Canonically**, Israel's exclusive God confession and John's Christological presentation should be related through actual allusions and actions. Distinguish ordinary Greek *egō eimi* identifications from marked statements, and keep the predicative or absolute syntax in view. **Limit:** proposed direct intertexts for each Johannine “I am” saying remain passage-level arguments, not a uniform dictionary classification.
theology_check: Discuss monotheistic confession and Christological reception from the full textual argument, not from an isolated numeral or phrase.

title: Creation, disorder, new creation
original_terms: Hebrew בָּרָא (bara), תֹּהוּ (tohu), בֹּהוּ (bohu), the phrase tohu wabohu; Greek κτίζω (ktizō), κτίσις (ktisis), καινός (kainos).
default_explanation: Bara alone does not state every philosophical claim about creation, and the presence of a creation word does not settle chronology or a scientific model.
translation_key: Explain unordered, uninhabited, or waste/void imagery from each passage. Preserve wild and waste as a proposed explanatory rendering, not a universal definition.
initial_orientation: Genesis 1:1-3 introduces creation and the earth's initial condition. Isaiah 45:18 contrasts an uninhabitable condition with habitation. Jeremiah 4:23 reuses creation language within judgment imagery. Second Corinthians 5:17 concerns new creation in Christ.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Bara, tohu, and bohu describe different aspects of creation or its condition. Genesis 1:1–5 introduces God's creative action, the earth's initial state, darkness, waters, and the ordering of light. Bara in a creation use does not independently specify the material mechanism, the duration of the process, or a complete philosophical account of creation from nothing. The narrative's clauses must provide the explanation.

The Hebrew lexicon also distinguishes homonymous or related bara records; a shared Strong number is not sufficient to choose the creation sense. Tohu can concern emptiness, waste, confusion, or futility in different contexts. Bohu is associated with emptiness in the limited phrase settings where it occurs. “Formless and empty” is a useful working rendering for Genesis 1:2, but its English words should not become universal scientific definitions of the Hebrew terms.

Isaiah 45:18 concerns God's purpose in creating the earth for habitation. Jeremiah 4:19–28 evokes an undone creation within judgment imagery. Their relation to Genesis is worth explaining, but Jeremiah's vision does not establish an earlier chronological event between Genesis 1:1 and 1:2. Shared wording and reversed creation imagery support literary interpretation, not an automatic reconstruction of an otherwise unstated prehistoric catastrophe.

#### Translation and default explanation

Use create, waste, empty, or another warranted rendering from the actual construction. Retain tohu wabohu in a note when the phrase's interpretation matters. Distinguish the Hebrew verb's stem and context; do not count a homonym as another example of creating. For Greek ktisis, distinguish the act of creation from created reality and relevant institutional or collective uses.

The default explanation is that creation language affirms God as the agent and source of the world as described, while a word's meaning alone does not decide modern scientific models or every metaphysical claim. Romans 4:17 and Hebrews 11:3 contribute further statements about God's action and the world's origin; those statements should be read directly rather than claimed as meanings hidden inside bara.

#### Biblical and canonical development

Second Corinthians 5:17 links being in Christ with new creation in an argument about reconciliation. Revelation 21:1–5 depicts new heaven and earth and renewed divine dwelling. These passages give a creation-to-renewal trajectory, but the adjective kainos cannot alone prove how much physical continuity or replacement occurs. Its contrast with neos is useful as a tendency, not an absolute rule.

The working synthesis connects God's ordering and life-giving purpose with the renewal promised in Christ. A theology review should distinguish creation's goodness, judgment's undoing, and renewed creation rather than treating them as one timeless metaphor. Explain a supported literary link before making a historical or doctrinal inference. For Genesis 1:1–2:3, recognize the completed literary unit under the translation scope exception; do not expand into two full chapters.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: create, emptiness and newness

This hub joins **distinct forms**: Hebrew **בָּרָא (*bara’*, create)**, **תֹּהוּ (*tohu*, wasteness/unformed disorder)**, **בֹּהוּ (*bohu*)**, and the expressive pairing **tohu va-bohu**; Greek **κτίζω (*ktizō*)**, **κτίσις (*ktisis*)** and **καινός (*kainos*, new in quality)**. They do not denote the same event or encode the entire doctrine of creation *ex nihilo* as their lexical definition.

**Usage by discourse.** Gen 1:1–3 describes the initial scene and Yahweh ordering the world; Hebrew *tohu va-bohu* can be rendered “wild and waste” while noting its poetic intensification. Isa 45:18 explicitly contrasts a world made **not for tohu** with one formed for habitation, clarifying functionality without asserting a universal physical-science lexicon. Jer 4:23 uses creation-disorder wording in a prophetic judgment scene: the poet imagines **de-creation**, not necessarily a second literal account of primordial cosmology. 2 Cor 5:17 uses *kainē ktisis* of new creation in Christ; its referent and newness arise from the discourse on reconciliation.

**Literary and historical controls.** Ancient Near Eastern creation narratives and cosmic-temple readings offer illuminating comparisons when specific motif and text are actually supplied; they are not proof that Gen 1 is a word-for-word translation of a temple ritual. “When God began to create” and “In the beginning God created” reflect syntactic interpretation, not a fixed meaning of *bara’*. **Canonically**, God's establishment of ordered, life-bearing creation and renewal through Christ form a strong thematic trajectory. **Limit:** a full philological argument about Genesis 1:1 syntax and all Hebrew *bara’* attestations demands focused textual analysis beyond a single hub.
theology_check: Trace ordering, habitation, de-creation imagery, and renewal, distinguishing direct wording from a proposed theological pattern.

title: Covenant and covenant instruction
original_terms: Hebrew בְּרִית (berit), תּוֹרָה (torah); Greek διαθήκη (diathēkē), νόμος (nomos). Covenant and instruction are related subjects, not synonyms.
default_explanation: Berit and diathēkē are not universally interchangeable merely because the latter often renders the former. Covenant relationship does not erase commands or promises.
translation_key: Use covenant or, where the setting requires, testament/will for diathēkē. Explain Torah as instruction in its setting instead of assuming every law reference means one identical legal system.
initial_orientation: Genesis 15 concerns promise and covenant enactment. Exodus 24 concerns ratification at Sinai. Jeremiah 31 announces a new covenant and inward instruction. Hebrews 8 quotes that announcement in its argument about Jesus' ministry.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Berit concerns covenant, agreement, or a binding relational arrangement, while torah concerns instruction or law. Their frequent connection does not make them synonyms. Genesis 15:1–18 places covenant-making within a promise to Abraham and a symbolic rite. Exodus 24:1–8 includes words, communal assent, and blood in the establishment of a covenant relation. The particular promises, commitments, and participants are necessary to explain each scene.

Torah may identify an instruction, priestly teaching, or a larger body of authoritative instruction. Calling it “instruction” can correct the impression that every occurrence means a modern statute book, but it must not weaken the binding force of commands where the text gives them. Psalm 1:1–3 depicts meditation on Yahweh's torah as a formative way of life, rather than the opposition of all law to all grace.

Jeremiah 31:31–34 promises a new covenant with Israel and Judah, contrasting it with the covenant broken by their ancestors and describing instruction written within, knowledge of God, and forgiveness. Hebrews 8:6–13 cites that promise in its argument about Christ's mediation. The quoted identification of the parties remains part of the source context even when a Christian account discusses wider participation. Hebrews 9:15–22 raises further questions because diathēkē can function in covenant and testament reasoning; the argument cannot be settled by insisting that Greek usage has only one permissible sense.

#### Translation and default explanation

Use covenant for berit in the relevant biblical arrangements, with enough explanation to identify the relation. Retain Torah with an instruction/law gloss where useful. For nomos, identify whether the author means Mosaic law, a scriptural collection, a principle, or another local use. Do not replace every nomos with Torah when the construction supports a different sense.

The default explanation is that covenant combines relationship with specified commitments, promises, and responsibilities. “Relationship” does not mean an arrangement without commands, and “law” does not mean an impersonal system disconnected from God's people. A theological contrast between covenants must come from their actual provisions and the author's argument.

#### Biblical and canonical development

The useful trajectory follows promise, covenant formation, covenant failure, and promised renewal through Christ. Luke 22:19–20 connects Jesus' blood with new-covenant language. Matthew 5:17–20 adds an important challenge to explanations that describe fulfillment as simple dismissal of the earlier Scriptures.

The working synthesis holds continuity of God's purpose together with changes asserted in the new-covenant texts. It should specify which commands, institutions, or promises the passage discusses rather than announce that everything is either unchanged or abolished. Theology review asks whether the explanation accounts for mediation, forgiveness, inward renewal, and the relationship between earlier and later textual settings. Keep covenant and instruction linked while retaining distinct lexical records and retrieval paths.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: covenant and instruction are not synonyms

Hebrew **בְּרִית (*berit*)** designates an agreement/covenant or binding relational arrangement; **תּוֹרָה (*torah*)** can mean instruction, teaching or law depending on object and setting. Greek **διαθήκη (*diathēkē*)** frequently represents covenant but can be pressed into testament/will-related reasoning in relevant contexts; **νόμος (*nomos*)** can be Mosaic law, a particular command, scriptural collection or more general ordering/standard. Neither a shared English term nor their presence in a theological scheme makes them lexically identical.

**Parties and obligations.** Gen 15 involves Yahweh's promise to Abraham and covenant enactment; Exod 24 features Moses, Israel, covenant words, assent and blood. Ps 1's delight in *torah* names formative instruction, not a denial of binding commands. Jer 31:31–34 explicitly identifies Israel and Judah, a broken former covenant, internalized instruction, knowledge of God and forgiveness. Heb 8 quotes and argues from that passage; a Christian account of participation must preserve the parties named in Jeremiah even while examining Christ's mediating role.

**Difficult Greek construction.** Heb 9:15–22 plays on *diathēkē* and questions of death, covenant and testamentary force. No universal gloss “covenant only” or “will only” can decide its logic without sentence-level exegesis. **Theological synthesis:** promise, faithful response, instruction, covenant breach and promised renewal are real canonical stages, not new lexical senses of *berit*. “Torah means only loving teaching and never law” is as reductive as “Torah is merely a modern statutory code.” **Limit:** this is a paired conceptual hub; its source words need independent semantic inventories in particular ancient legal genres.
theology_check: Keep covenant parties, promises, obligations, signs, and fulfillment distinct while tracing development.

title: Love, ahavah, agapē
original_terms: Hebrew אַהֲבָה (ahavah), אָהַב (ahav); Greek ἀγάπη (agapē), ἀγαπάω (agapaō), φιλέω (phileō). Separate senses and forms.
default_explanation: Agapē is not automatically a technical term for divine, morally perfect love, and agapaō/phileō should not receive an inflexible contrast in every occurrence.
translation_key: Translate love while identifying its object, relationships, and actions. Explain self-giving from the relevant descriptions rather than treating it as a meaning built into every agap- form.
initial_orientation: Deuteronomy and Leviticus concern love of God and neighbor. John 3:19 uses the love verb with darkness as its object. John 13 shapes love by Jesus' example. First Corinthians 13 describes love's conduct.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Love vocabulary can express affection, commitment, preference, or practical concern according to its object and setting. Deuteronomy 6:4–5 concerns love of Yahweh within a summons to exclusive allegiance. Leviticus 19:18 places neighbor-love beside commands about hostility, revenge, and the treatment of others. These contexts establish the required orientation and conduct; the Hebrew root alone does not supply the whole ethical explanation.

Agapē and agapaō are important in Christian texts but are not automatic labels for morally perfect divine love. John 3:19 uses agapaō for people's loving darkness rather than light. The object and the surrounding judgment make that love wrongful. A translation theory that assigns every occurrence a uniquely selfless divine sense cannot account for this use without changing its own rule.

John 13:34–35 gives Jesus' love as the pattern for the disciples' love and as a public mark of discipleship. First Corinthians 13:1–7 explains love through contrasts and descriptions within a discussion of communal gifts. Its claims about patience, kindness, boasting, and harm come from the paragraph's predicates; they are not all dictionary content encoded in the noun agapē. First John 4:7–12 grounds the communal summons in God's action through the Son.

#### Translation and default explanation

“Love” is usually a sound starting point, with a note identifying the object and expression. Dutch *liefde* and *liefhebben* require the same local attention. Retaining agapē can be useful in a study, but it should not imply that English or Dutch lacks any meaningful equivalent.

The default explanation is that biblical writers give love a particular moral shape through God's character, commands, and actions. The word alone is not that entire shape. Phileō overlaps with loving language and can also describe kissing. John 11:3–5 uses both phileō and agapaō in the account of Jesus and Lazarus' household. John 21:15–19 alternates them while also varying other vocabulary. A proposed distinction may be discussed, but a rigid “divine love versus merely human friendship” contrast should not be presented as an established lexical rule.

#### Biblical and canonical development

A focused trajectory connects whole-person love of God, neighbor-love, Jesus' self-giving example, and renewed communal practice. Matthew 5:43–48 extends the ethical comparison to enemies, providing a concrete test of interpretations that reduce love to warmth toward one's own group.

The working synthesis sees love as central to faithful life, with its content specified by these texts. It does not treat any strong feeling or desire as morally valid simply because someone calls it love. Theology review should distinguish the source word's local use from the evaluation of its object and expression. Link loyal love, mercy, faith, and marriage where relevant; do not retrieve all four automatically for every occurrence of agapē.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: love across different objects

Hebrew **אָהַב (*’ahav*, love)** and **אַהֲבָה (*’ahavah*, love)**, Greek **ἀγαπάω (*agapaō*)**, **ἀγάπη (*agapē*)**, and **φιλέω (*phileō*)** have overlapping but distinct distributions. Do not assert that *agapē* by itself always denotes uniquely divine, unconditional, morally perfect love while *phileō* always means inferior friendship. The object of love and author's judgment of that object matter.

**Contextual contrasts.** Deut 6:5 commands wholehearted love of Yahweh, embedded in obedience and teaching. Lev 19:18 concerns neighbour relationships and refuses revenge. John 3:19 describes people who **loved darkness rather than light**: the *agapaō* word family can denote wrongly directed preference. John 13:34–35 frames mutual love by Jesus' own demonstrated action, giving moral specificity from **His example**, not from the bare verb. 1 Cor 13 lists love's patience, non-envy and endurance as part of Paul's argument to a divided community, rather than claiming that every occurrence of *agapē* secretly contains the whole chapter.

**Connections and boundaries.** *Ḥesed* may be a type of reliable loving kindness but is not simply another generic word for love; *eleos* emphasizes mercy, and *charis* may denote favor or grace. Jesus' command, loving action and self-giving provide a theological account of love, not a license to replace every *agapē* with one rigid formula. **Limit:** the metaphorical erotic, familial, preferential and hostile-object contexts of all five lemmas exceed the selected examples; avoid unfounded claims based on word roots.
theology_check: Trace commanded love, divine love, and Christ's example without exporting every positive description into negative-object uses.

title: Hesed, loyal love, kindness
original_terms: Hebrew חֶסֶד (ḥesed/chesed/khesed), H2617; distinguish ordinary positive kindness/loyal-love usage from the separate same-spelling shame/reproach homonym. Greek translations must be checked per verse.
default_explanation: Explain the complete attested positive semantic range, then select a context-specific emphasis, then present canonical/theological interpretation. The noun does not mean love + mercy + grace + loyalty + covenant simultaneously. Divine constancy is a claim about God's character, not a different lexical definition. Covenant Love is contextual/theological, not compulsory in every occurrence.
translation_key: Contextually choose generous goodness, kindness, mercy/barmhartigheid, protective concern, loyalty, steadfast/trouwe liefde, or covenant love/verbondsliefde when explicit. Grace/genade is sometimes a connotation rather than the ordinary direct gloss. Keep ḥen, ḥannun, raḥum, ’emet, berit and Greek eleos/charis lexically distinct, and separate the H2617 shame/reproach homonym.
initial_orientation: Exod 34:6-7: Yahweh's abundant hesed following covenant betrayal. Hos 6:4-6: Israel's fleeting human hesed against Yahweh's desire. Ps 136: Yahweh's enduring hesed. Josh 2, Ruth 3, 1 Sam 20 and 2 Sam 9: human-to-human kindness and pledged loyalty.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Hesed commonly concerns kindness, loyalty, or generous committed concern in a relationship. Exodus 34:6–7 places it within Yahweh's self-description after covenant failure. Its abundance and connection with emet contribute to a portrait of dependable mercy. The surrounding statements about forgiveness and wrongdoing also matter: isolating “loyal love” from the unit can make the passage appear to deny judgment.

Ruth 3:10 uses hesed in Boaz's assessment of Ruth's conduct. Micah 6:8 requires the human hearer to love hesed alongside doing justice and walking humbly with God. These are direct checks against the claim that hesed is only action from a superior to an inferior or only a technical term for God's covenant. Genesis 19:19 concerns kindness shown to Lot, and First Samuel 20:12–17 connects loyal concern with a pledged relationship. A formal covenant may be relevant, but it must be shown in the passage rather than inserted into every use.

The lexical identifiers reveal a further distinction: the Open Scriptures index has separate H2617-linked records for kindness and for shame or reproach. Leviticus 20:17 provides an important disambiguation setting. The fact that the records share spelling and a base Strong number must not make the plugin transfer the kindness sense into a condemnation. The kindness record OSHB:ecp and the reproach record OSHB:eco remain separate in this package.

#### Translation and default explanation

“Kindness,” “loyal love,” “steadfast love,” or a retained hesed with an explanatory gloss may fit different passages. “Covenant loyalty” can be useful when the relation and conduct support it, but it is stronger than a neutral one-word gloss. Dutch *trouwe liefde* or *goedertierenheid* likewise requires an explanation appropriate to the reader and setting.

The default explanation is that hesed often describes reliable or generous kindness expressed within relationships. It is not one fixed legal formula, a term used only of God, or a guarantee that every beneficiary has an identical covenant status. A Greek counterpart must be checked in the particular LXX passage; selecting eleos everywhere from a general lexical description would conceal variation in ancient translation choices.

#### Biblical and canonical development

The useful trajectory connects God's continuing kindness after failure with the kindness expected among his people. Psalm 136's refrain develops the enduring quality of divine hesed through narrated acts. This is a literary and theological pattern, not evidence that the noun always means every act listed in the psalm.

The working synthesis emphasizes dependable relationship expressed in action and reads that pattern alongside justice and mercy. A theology review should ask whether a proposed interpretation identifies the parties and their actual obligations, and whether it allows the text's generosity without making it a contractual wage. Keep the homonym check explicit; this is an example where lexical databases improve accuracy beyond a clean English extract.
 
#### Full range, selection and theology — 2026-10-09 revision

Hesed has a contextual positive range of practical beneficent goodness or kindness, generous assistance, mercy to vulnerable people, loyal or affectionate concern, reliable love in close relationships, covenant loyalty where formally pledged, and sometimes human fidelity/devotion to Yahweh. These aspects overlap but are NOT automatically simultaneous. The inspected OSHB:ecp binding gives a partial BDB record for human kindness/mercy/piety and divine lovingkindness. The lexeme does not itself encode a covenant, unmerited grace, permanence, or God's complete moral character. Context decides.

Direct human cases: Gen 21:23 asks reciprocity; Gen 47:29 requests family loyalty; Josh 2:12-14 uses hesed for Rahab's protection and reciprocal protection by the spies, before their promise has been made; Ruth 1:8 and 3:10 describe loving family care; 1 Sam 20:14-17 is an explicit pledge and 2 Sam 9:1-3 its generous fulfilment. Thus 'covenant love' can fit pledged settings but is too narrow as a general definition. Gen 19:19 foregrounds mercy/rescue; Gen 24:27 joins hesed with ’emet, highlighting reliability. Deut 7:9 explicitly pairs covenant (berit) AND hesed, not conflating them.

Divine-human distinction is THEOLOGICAL, not a two-lemma rule: Exod 34:6-7 portrays Yahweh rich in steadfast kindness despite Exod 32's covenant breach, with accountability still intact. Ps 136 poetically repeats that His hesed endures. Hos 6:4 calls people's hesed evaporating dew; 6:6 says Yahweh desires it, alongside knowledge of God. Mic 6:8 commands loving hesed alongside doing justice and walking humbly. Humans really can show love, kindness, mercy and loyalty but need not sustain them; Yahweh is always faithful because of His revealed character. Do not smuggle God's indefectible faithfulness into every human occurrence.

Grace/mercy: Gen 19:19 places ḥen (favor, grace) AND hesed in one verse; Exod 34:6 distinguishes gracious (ḥannun), compassionate (raḥum), and rich in hesed. 'Grace' can be the undeserved theological effect of hesed, but not the one-to-one dictionary gloss; 'mercy' is directly represented by ancient Greek eleos in Ruth 3:10, Hos 6:6, Mic 6:8 and Ps 136 (Greek Ps 135). Ancient Greek Exod 34:6 uses polyeleos, while Gen 19:19 and 24:27 render hesed with dikaiosynē: translator equivalents must be investigated individually. Matt 9:13 and 12:7 explicitly quote Hos 6:6 using eleos; Luke 1 remembers divine mercy and covenant promises. John 1:14-17's grace-and-truth wording plausibly echoes Exod 34 in the Moses/glory context, not a direct charis = hesed dictionary equation.

Do not conflate positive hesed with the rare homonym in Lev 20:17, 'shame/disgrace' (OSHB:eco, partial BDB h.ee.ab; Greek oneidos). Prov 14:34 and Isa 40:6 require separate, cautious textual/lexical discussion; Isa 40:6's Greek speaks of glory/splendour, but this does not establish that the ordinary noun always means beauty. Full studies must expose such exceptions and uncertainties and distinguish lexical attestation, contextual nuance, and canonical theological synthesis.
theology_check: Check actor, relationship, context and action before glossing hesed; distinguish divine reliability (revealed character) and genuine but inconsistent human kindness. 'Covenant Love' is a useful covenant-specific synthesis, not universal lexical meaning. Separate mercy, grace and neighboring Hebrew/Greek terms. Preserve the shame homonym and ambiguous Isa 40:6.

title: Truth, reliability, faithfulness
original_terms: Hebrew אֱמֶת (emet), אֱמוּנָה (emunah); Greek ἀλήθεια (alētheia), πιστός (pistos). Keep truth and faith vocabulary linked but distinct.
default_explanation: Etymological relationships do not make every occurrence a complete theological definition of truth. A suggested Exodus/John link is a canonical argument, not literal identity of the words.
translation_key: Decide between truth, reliability, and faithfulness from the actual claim and construction; record the precise term present before making an OT/NT connection.
initial_orientation: Exodus 34 places emet beside hesed. Psalm 89 sets divine love and faithfulness within a royal-covenant poem. John 1:14-18 concerns the Word, grace, truth, and the disclosure of God.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Emet and emunah can concern truth, dependability, fidelity, or firmness according to their construction. Their relationship to trust vocabulary is useful, but deriving every sense from a root associated with firmness would erase actual usage. Greek alētheia and pistos contribute truth and faithfulness language without becoming interchangeable translations in every passage. A truthful statement, a reliable person, and covenant faithfulness are related ideas with different grammatical expressions.

Exodus 34:6–7 pairs hesed and emet within God's self-description. Dependable kindness is an appropriate explanatory emphasis in that setting, while truthfulness should not be excluded simply because a modern explanation prefers relational vocabulary. Psalm 89:1–2 introduces praise of God's loyal love and faithfulness; the wider psalm's treatment of promise and apparent failure gives these qualities a narrative and covenantal weight.

Deuteronomy 32:4 relates God's faithfulness to justice and freedom from wrongdoing. Psalm 119:142 places truth in relation to God's instruction. John 8:31–36 connects remaining in Jesus' word, knowing truth, and freedom. These texts do not oppose truthful content to trustworthy relationship. Romans 3:3–4 explicitly contrasts human unfaithfulness with God's faithfulness and truthfulness, demonstrating how the ideas interact within an argument rather than through a single universal gloss.

#### Translation and default explanation

Choose truth, faithfulness, reliability, or a qualified expression according to the subject and object. “Faithful” describes a person or action differently from “true” describing a statement; a natural target-language translation should preserve that difference. Dutch *waarheid*, *betrouwbaarheid*, and *trouw* similarly require contextual selection. Retain emet or emunah in a note when the shared English vocabulary hides a meaningful distinction.

The default explanation is that biblical truth includes correspondence with what is real and reliable integrity in relevant personal settings. It should not be reduced either to abstract propositions with no relation to conduct or to relationship with no concern for truthful statements. The source construction determines what is asserted locally.

#### Biblical and canonical development

John 1:14–18 describes the Word with grace and truth language. Comparison with Exodus 34 is a valuable canonical proposal because of the larger constellation of glory, divine disclosure, gracious character, and Moses. It is not proof that charis is literally the same lemma as hesed or that every Johannine truth occurrence is a direct citation of emet. Label this connection as a reasoned literary and theological relationship rather than an exact lexical identity.

The working synthesis follows God's dependability, trustworthy revelation, and human life shaped by truth. It should explain how the selected passage joins belief, speech, and conduct. Theology review asks whether an account of faithfulness allows the text's statements about wrongdoing, justice, and promised action to retain their force. The presence of a truth word alone cannot resolve the factual or theological claim made by the surrounding sentence; that claim still requires interpretation and, where relevant, textual comparison.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: truth and reliability

Hebrew **אֱמֶת (*’emet*)** can indicate truth, factual veracity, dependability, faithfulness and reliability depending on clause; **אֱמוּנָה (*’emunah*)** more often draws attention to steadfastness, fidelity or trustworthy support. Greek **ἀλήθεια (*alētheia*)** commonly indicates truth/reality, and **πιστός (*pistos*)** describes faithful or believing persons depending on referent. These overlap but are not synonyms or universal replacements for one another.

**Participants and pairings.** Exod 34:6 pairs Yahweh's *hesed* with *’emet* in a declaration following Israel's unfaithfulness. There “reliability/faithfulness” fits because Yahweh is the characterized speaker and the context is covenant repair; this does not prove *’emet* always means “covenant fidelity.” Psalm 89 connects God's faithfulness with Davidic promise and royal lament, inviting analysis of the addressed God and uncertain human political outcome. John 1:14–18 says Christ is full of grace and truth in a scene recalling Moses and divine disclosure. “Truth” there is not reduced to factual accuracy alone, but the wider revelatory claim comes from the prologue, not from the lexeme.

**Translation and canonical reasoning.** In a testimony setting “truth” may be best; in a promise/character context “faithfulness” or “reliability” may communicate the point. Dutch *waarheid*, *trouw* and *betrouwbaarheid* require the same caution. Opposing “truth” to “love” as if *’emet* denotes cold information ignores the literary collocations. **Limit:** a complete concordance of truth-claims, legal testimony, honesty and enduring faithfulness has not been assembled; some contexts warrant live alternatives.
theology_check: Trace the reliability of God and His promises and distinguish that trajectory from the meaning of each local term.

title: Grace, favor, graciousness
original_terms: Hebrew חֵן (chen), חַנּוּן (channun), חָנַן (chanan); Greek χάρις (charis). Record noun, adjective, and verb separately.
default_explanation: A source discussing chen as a word family must not cause the adjective channun in Exodus 34:6 to be mislabeled as that noun. Grace does not lexically mean every later definition of unmerited favor in every context.
translation_key: Use favor, grace, gracious, or related wording according to grammar and relationship. Explain theological implications through the passage's argument.
initial_orientation: Genesis 6:8 speaks of Noah finding favor. Exodus 34:6 uses the adjective channun in the description of Yahweh. Ephesians 2:8-10 relates grace to salvation, faith, and good works.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Grace vocabulary includes favor, gracious action, and the effects or response associated with a gift. Hebrew chen is a noun, channun an adjective, and chanan a verb. Exodus 34:6 uses channun in God's self-description; it must not be tagged as an occurrence of the noun chen merely because the words are related. That distinction matters for exact-form retrieval and for an interlinear that represents what is actually on the page.

Genesis 6:8 describes Noah finding favor in Yahweh's eyes in a narrative of widespread corruption and impending judgment. The phrase identifies favorable regard; the wider narrative supplies its moral and saving setting. Genesis 33:8–11 uses favor language in a human relationship, showing why the noun's basic range cannot be reduced to a technical doctrine of conversion.

Ephesians 2:8–10 makes grace central to salvation as gift and excludes boasting. Romans 4:4–5 contrasts grace with a wage owed. In these contexts, freeness is strongly supported by the argument. Titus 2:11–14 also presents grace as teaching a changed way of life. Romans 6:1–2 rejects using grace as permission to continue in sin. These passages provide the theological account through their assertions; a lexicon cannot make the ethical teaching disappear by glossing the noun as favor.

#### Translation and default explanation

Use grace, favor, gracious, or show favor according to the form and setting. Dutch *genade*, *gunst*, and *genadig* are useful distinctions. If grace is a familiar church word but obscure to the reader, explain the particular generous action or favorable regard rather than adding an entire doctrinal definition inside the translation.

The default explanation is that God's saving grace is freely given in the relevant New Testament arguments and produces a new orientation of life. “Unmerited favor” summarizes an important theological claim in those contexts, but it is not the exhaustive meaning of every charis or chen occurrence. Charis can also concern gratitude or a gracious quality in other constructions. The actual source record must remain open to those uses.

#### Biblical and canonical development

The useful trajectory connects God's gracious character, favor shown in the saving narrative, and salvation and renewed conduct in Christ. Exodus 34 and Ephesians 2 can illuminate that trajectory, but their forms and contexts remain distinct. A project explanation should not count the adjective in Exodus as evidence for the noun's occurrence frequency.

The working synthesis joins gift and transformation without turning transformation into a wage that precedes the gift. Theology review asks whether a claim identifies salvation's source, reception, and intended result accurately. Good works in Ephesians 2:10 belong to the argument and must not be omitted from a grace study; verses 8–9 also must not be softened into a generic encouragement to try harder. Keep the grace, works, faith, and sanctification records linked for these specific comparisons.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: grace, favour and graciousness

**Forms and core ranges:** Hebrew **חֵן (*ḥen*)** denotes favour, gracious regard or attractiveness in some social settings; **חָנַן (*ḥanan*)** is a verb of showing favour or being gracious; **חַנּוּן (*ḥannun*)** is a gracious adjective. Greek **χάρις (*charis*)** ranges across favour, generosity/grace, gift-related beneficence and in certain constructions gratitude or thanks. These are related but morphologically distinct and not interchangeable at each occurrence.

**Contextual controls.** Gen 6:8 says Noah found *ḥen* in Yahweh's eyes within the judgment narrative; God is the one who shows favour, but the phrase does not itself encode a complete doctrine of predestination. Gen 33:8–11 uses favour language between humans, showing that its ordinary range is not exclusively salvific. Exod 34:6 calls Yahweh **ḥannun**, not the noun *ḥen*, within a string also containing compassion and *ḥesed*: these terms illuminate one another without becoming synonyms. Eph 2:8–10 portrays salvation as gift excluding boastful earning, with good works explicitly given their proper place as intended result. Rom 4:4–5 uses wages as a foil for unearned gift. Titus 2:11–14 personifies grace as teaching changed conduct.

**Mercy and hesed boundary.** Mercy (*eleos*, barmhartigheid/ontferming) often emphasizes aid to a distressed party; *hesed* can emphasize beneficent love or fidelity; *charis/ḥen* often favour or giving, but the overlap is real. “Unmerited favour” is a useful *theological* explanation in specified saving contexts, not an exhaustive dictionary meaning of every *charis*. **Limit:** civil/social gratitude and charm uses require additional verified examples before claiming a complete corpus map.
theology_check: Compare divine generosity, favor, and salvation while keeping ordinary social uses visible.

title: Compassion and mercy
original_terms: Hebrew רַחוּם (rachum), רַחֲמִים (rachamim); Greek ἔλεος (eleos), σπλαγχνίζομαι (splanchnizomai). These are related resources, not fixed translation equivalents.
default_explanation: A proposed root relationship with womb is not proof that a womb image is active in every use of compassion vocabulary.
translation_key: Retain compassionate or merciful wording that fits the actual term; use bodily or parental imagery as explanation where the passage supplies it.
initial_orientation: Exodus 34 describes Yahweh as compassionate. Isaiah 49:15 uses maternal imagery to express God's remembrance. Luke 10 depicts compassion becoming practical aid in the Samaritan narrative.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Compassion and mercy vocabulary expresses responsive concern, pity, or kindness, often toward someone in distress. Rachum is a Hebrew adjective; rachamim is a related noun form; eleos is Greek mercy language; splanchnizomai describes being moved with compassion. Their association does not make them fixed one-to-one equivalents. The passage must supply the agent, the need, and the response.

Exodus 34:6–7 places compassion within God's self-description after covenant failure. Psalm 103:8–14 explains divine compassion through patience, forgiveness, and the comparison of a father's concern for children, with humanity's frailty in view. These surrounding claims make the image concrete. Hosea 11:1–9 uses parent-child language in a painful account of Israel's response and God's announced restraint; its literary movement should not be reduced to a detached dictionary slogan.

Isaiah 49:15 explicitly compares God's remembrance with a mother's relation to her nursing child. A maternal connection can therefore be argued directly in this passage. It does not follow that every racham-related occurrence is a hidden womb metaphor. The lexical database distinguishes a womb record from compassion records even where base identifiers or word families overlap. Historical association and active contextual imagery are different kinds of evidence.

#### Translation and default explanation

Use compassionate, merciful, pity, or an action-oriented expression as the clause warrants. “Moved with compassion” can preserve the emotional movement of splanchnizomai while a note explains the bodily idiom if useful. A literal organ or womb gloss should not replace the understood sense in ordinary prose.

The default explanation is that mercy often involves concern translated into action, while the particular action must be read from the narrative. In Luke 10:25–37, the Samaritan's compassion leads to care, transport, and provision; the final question identifies the neighbor through doing mercy. Matthew 9:35–38 connects Jesus' compassion with distressed crowds and a summons concerning workers. These texts define concrete responses rather than mere sympathetic feeling.

#### Biblical and canonical development

A focused trajectory connects God's compassionate character with the mercy expected from those who know him. James 2:13–17 relates mercy, judgment, and the inadequacy of kind words without practical aid. That is a useful bridge to the faith-and-works question when the user's passage concerns treatment of the vulnerable.

The working synthesis treats mercy as morally serious and relationally concrete. It does not erase judgment or make mercy an emotional disposition with no action. A theology review asks whether the interpretation honors the need and response actually described, and whether its social or doctrinal application is supported by the passage. Do not import every maternal image into every mercy term; use Isaiah's explicit comparison where that particular explanation helps. Keep kindness, grace, and mercy linked without collapsing their lexical records.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: compassion, pity, mercy

Hebrew **רַחוּם (*raḥum*)** is a compassionate/merciful adjective; **רַחֲמִים (*raḥamim*)** relates to mercy or compassion; Greek **ἔλεος (*eleos*)** can describe mercy, pity or practical kindness; **σπλαγχνίζομαι (*splanchnizomai*)** describes being moved with compassion. They are distinct words even when applied to the same event. The historical *raḥam* / womb association must not be projected as an active maternal image into every token without literary evidence.

**Agents and effects.** Exod 34:6 calls Yahweh compassionate **and** gracious **and** rich in *hesed*, so these are overlapping parts of His revealed character, not one fused lemma. Ps 103:8–14 attributes patient, parental compassion to God toward vulnerable humans; the father's comparison belongs to this psalm. Isa 49:15 **explicitly** compares God's remembrance to a nursing mother, giving a solid local basis for maternal imagery. In Luke 10:25–37 the Samaritan feels compassion and responds through treatment, transport and ongoing care; the wounded traveller is the concrete beneficiary, and neighbouring religious figures do not provide that help. Matt 9:35–38 depicts Jesus' compassion at distressed crowds, leading into His concern for labourers.

**Related ideas and limits.** “Mercy,” “grace,” “love” and “hesed” overlap in divine action but are not always interchangeable Greek/Hebrew word equivalents. Divine compassion does not mean indifference to judgment: James 2:13 discusses mercy and judgment together. **Limit:** bodily idiom, maternal metaphor and legal “show mercy” formulas require occurrence-level checks rather than universal word-root claims.

title: Anger, patience, slow to anger
original_terms: Hebrew אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (erekh appayim); Greek ὀργή (orgē), μακροθυμία (makrothymia). An idiom and several nouns require separate records.
default_explanation: Slow to anger does not mean no judgment, and a literal nose gloss should not replace the idiom's sense in a working translation.
translation_key: Translate the Hebrew idiom idiomatically and explain its literal wording in a note. Identify anger, wrath, patience, and forbearance rather than collapsing them.
initial_orientation: Exodus 34 includes slow to anger among God's qualities. Proverbs 14:29 contrasts patience and quick temper. Romans 2:4 places patience and kindness beside repentance and judgment.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Erekh appayim is a Hebrew idiom conventionally rendered “slow to anger.” Its component words involve length and nose/anger vocabulary, but the phrase's communicated sense concerns patience or restraint. A source-order interlinear can show the components while a readable translation gives the idiom. Translating it merely as “long of nostrils” without explanation would leave most readers with an inaccurate impression.

Exodus 34:6–7 places patience alongside compassion, grace, loyal love, faithfulness, forgiveness, and the treatment of wrongdoing. The portrait cannot be reduced either to anger without patience or to patience without judgment. Numbers 14:17–20 reuses these qualities within Moses' appeal after Israel's failure, demonstrating their significance for a concrete covenant crisis rather than only as a list of attributes.

Proverbs 14:29 relates slowness to anger with understanding. Its practical setting concerns human conduct and discernment, not an exhaustive doctrine of divine emotion. Romans 2:4–5 describes God's kindness and patience as leading toward repentance while warning against hardness that stores up wrath. The transition is part of the argument: patience is purposeful and morally consequential, not proof that wrongdoing has become inconsequential.

#### Translation and default explanation

Render the idiom as slow to anger, patient, or a target-language expression with the same force. Dutch *lankmoedig* may require explanation; *langzaam tot toorn* preserves the familiar biblical shape but may be less natural for some readers. Record the source components without treating a literal gloss as the idiom's whole meaning.

The default explanation is that biblical patience describes restraint and endurance in the relevant relationship, allowing time for response. It does not entail absence of anger or judgment. Greek orgē concerns anger or wrath; makrothymia concerns patience or forbearance. A shared context does not make them opposites in every possible sense or justify assigning one only to humans and the other only to God.

#### Biblical and canonical development

Psalm 103:8–14 relates divine patience to compassion and human frailty. Second Peter 3:8–10 places patience within a response to questions about the promised coming and judgment. These provide a focused trajectory concerning delay, opportunity, and fulfillment. The text's announced judgment must remain visible even when an explanation emphasizes the generosity of the delay.

The working synthesis portrays God's response to evil as purposeful rather than impulsive, while allowing the passages' particular claims about anger to stand. A theology review should distinguish the communicated human idiom from conclusions about the mechanics of divine emotional experience. Modern psychological descriptions may illustrate an application but cannot become the translation. For human conduct, patience is not passivity toward harm: the passage's context must identify what restraint, justice, and appropriate action require.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: anger and restrained anger

Hebrew **אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם (*’erekh ’appayim*)** is an idiom literally involving length of nostrils/anger and conventionally describes being **slow to anger**; Greek **ὀργή (*orgē*)** refers to anger or wrath, and **μακροθυμία (*makrothymia*)** to patience/long-suffering. They are related topics, not interchangeable lemmas. “Slow to anger” does not mean never opposing evil, and “wrath” does not by itself specify how long or by what means judgment is enacted.

**Textual participants and moral direction.** In Exod 34:6–7 Yahweh's patience is spoken after Israel's grave unfaithfulness; it appears beside compassion, *hesed*, forgiveness and accountable judgment. Prov 14:29 contrasts the person who restrains anger with the quick-tempered person; humans are responsible agents, not objects of an abstract temperament test. Rom 2:4–5 describes God's kindness and patience as intended to lead a human audience toward repentance; that audience's stubborn response builds up judgment. The text therefore juxtaposes patience and wrath within one argument rather than making them contradict.

**Historical and theological boundaries.** Ancient anger idioms can be translated naturally in modern language while retaining an explanatory note where the body metaphor matters. God's patience belongs to His character but is not a lexically implied guarantee of infinite delay. Human anger can be morally evaluated by motive, proportion and conduct. A theology of God's justice and compassion must come from the passages' claims, not the invented etymology of Greek *orgē*. **Limit:** individual anger idioms and difficult “divine repentance” contexts need passage-specific review.
theology_check: Read patience and moral judgment together rather than using either to cancel the other.

title: Hear, listen, obey
original_terms: Hebrew שָׁמַע (shama, shema as the command form); Greek ἀκούω (akouō), ὑπακούω (hypakouō).
default_explanation: The word family can include attentive response, but that does not make auditory hearing and obedience identical in every occurrence.
translation_key: Use hear, listen, heed, or obey where syntax and response establish the use. Explain the relation between reception and action without changing every hear verb into obey.
initial_orientation: Deuteronomy 6 begins with a summons to hear within instruction to love and teach. First Samuel 15:22 contrasts obedience and sacrifice. James 1 distinguishes hearing the word from doing it.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Shama can concern hearing, attending, listening responsively, or obeying. Shema in Deuteronomy 6:4 is a command form, not a separate dictionary lemma whose meaning automatically differs from the verb family. The summons introduces a confession and whole-person love, followed by the repeated teaching and remembrance of God's words in ordinary life. Reading the command within verses 4–9 makes its responsive force clear.

First Samuel 15:22 contrasts obedience with sacrificial performance in the setting of Saul's failure. Here listening cannot be reduced to auditory perception: the contrast concerns responding to Yahweh's instruction. That contextual force does not mean every shama occurrence lexically entails obedience. Isaiah 6:9–10 speaks of hearing without understanding in a prophetic commission, showing why the senses and effects need to remain distinguishable.

Greek akouō likewise concerns hearing or listening in varied constructions. Hypakouō often concerns obedient response, but its range includes answering a knock at the door. A lexical database preserves these separate records and their settings. Mark 4:1–9's repeated hearing summons belongs to a parable whose narrative concerns varied reception; a theology of response comes from that developing argument rather than from a prefix alone.

#### Translation and default explanation

Use hear, listen, heed, or obey where the construction and contrast support it. “Hear, Israel” preserves the traditional opening of Deuteronomy 6; a note can explain that attentive response is expected. Translating it as “Obey, Israel” may express an aspect of the summons but obscures the speech-event metaphor and should not be treated as the only literal rendering.

The default explanation is that biblical listening often seeks understanding and response, yet hearing and obedience are not automatically identical senses. James 1:19–25 explicitly moves from readiness to hear toward doing the word and warns against hearing alone. That distinction should remain intelligible. Replacing every hear with obey would make the letter's contrast harder to explain and could falsely imply obedience has already occurred whenever someone hears.

#### Biblical and canonical development

The useful trajectory follows God's address, the people's reception, and embodied response. Romans 10:14–17 connects proclamation, hearing, and faith; it gives a concrete account of how the message is encountered. Deuteronomy's teaching pattern provides another route where family, memory, and daily practice are relevant.

The working synthesis treats attention to God's word as a summons to faithful response, not merely information acquisition. A theology review should ask what the passage says about understanding, willingness, and action, and should not assume the presence of the hearing verb answers all three questions. For an application, identify what is being heard and what response the unit actually asks for. Link heart, faith, and word entries only when they clarify those relations rather than as an automatic cluster loaded for every hearing occurrence.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: hearing and response

Hebrew **שָׁמַע (*shama‘*)** ranges across perceiving sound, listening attentively, hearing testimony, accepting a message and obeying a voice in constructions where the object and discourse support that consequence. Greek **ἀκούω (*akouō*)** means hear/listen and can involve responsive reception; **ὑπακούω (*hypakouō*)** more explicitly involves obedience or heeding. The imperative **Shema** in Deut 6:4 is a form of *shama‘*, not a separate mystical lexical root.

**Contextual evidence.** Deut 6:4–9 addresses Israel to hear Yahweh's confession and love Him wholeheartedly, continuing into teaching and remembering commands. Its *whole discourse* gives obedience as the proper response; saying the verb always means “obey” erases ordinary acoustic uses. 1 Sam 15:22 contrasts Samuel's call to hearken/obey with sacrificial activity as Saul is rebuked. James 1:22–25 explicitly distinguishes hearing from doing, providing strong evidence that the two are not lexically identical even where real hearing properly leads to action.

**Translation and synthesis.** “Hear,” “listen,” “heed,” and “obey” may all be appropriate in different clauses, depending on the subject's relation to the speaker, the imperative or report, and the actual behaviour. A sermon explaining that “biblical hearing demands obedient attention” may be sound theology while still wrong as a claim that the phonetic root means “obey in every verse.” The canonical trajectory links revelation, covenant summons and responsive discipleship without pretending sound perception is never the intended use. **Limit:** specific court testimony, divine hearing of prayer and overhearing categories need their own checked references.
theology_check: Connect covenant hearing, prophetic summons, and discipleship through selected contexts.

title: Meod, strength, whole-person intensity
original_terms: Hebrew מְאֹד (meod); Greek ἰσχύς (ischys) and related strength vocabulary in relevant reception contexts. Verify each actual rendering.
default_explanation: Strength is a context-dependent rendering of this unusual construction, not the meaning to substitute wherever meod occurs.
translation_key: Translate the intensifier as very where appropriate. Explain all one's meod in the Shema instead of assuming a separate physical faculty.
initial_orientation: Genesis 1:31 uses meod as an intensifier in very good. Deuteronomy 6:5 places it after heart and nephesh in the command to love. Mark 12 quotes and develops the command with Greek vocabulary.
core_study:
#### Local reading

Meod is frequently an intensifier meaning very, greatly, or exceedingly. Genesis 1:31 describes what God has made as very good. Substituting “strength” for meod there would be inappropriate. Deuteronomy 6:5 uses it in an unusual nominal expression concerning loving Yahweh with all one's meod. This construction supports renderings such as might or strength, while the word's ordinary intensifying use remains relevant to explaining its force.

An illustrative rendering “with all your muchness” can help a learner notice the unusual Hebrew expression, but it is not natural working prose and should not masquerade as a settled exhaustive meaning. Interpretations involving all one's capacities or resources may illuminate the summons. They require an explanation of the phrase and its reception, not a claim that meod normally names wealth or muscular power.

Mark 12:28–34 places the command within a conversation about the greatest commandment and adds explicit mind language alongside heart, soul, and strength. Luke 10:25–28 also presents a fuller sequence. Second Kings 23:25 uses heart, nephesh, and meod language in describing Josiah's turning to Yahweh. These are useful reception and application contexts rather than evidence that every listed human faculty is a separate metaphysical component.

#### Translation and default explanation

For Deuteronomy 6:5, “with all your strength” or “with all your might” remains a reasonable working translation. Explain that the Hebrew employs a word commonly used to intensify, here substantivized in a whole-person summons. Dutch *met al je kracht* communicates the reception well; a study note can make the unusual source expression visible.

The default explanation is that the phrase calls for wholehearted commitment involving the person's available capacities. Strength is a contextual rendering here, not a universal gloss for meod. An interlinear should preserve the inflected form and the relationship of “all” to each expression, rather than producing an English faculty chart that the source does not supply.

#### Biblical and canonical development

The useful trajectory connects exclusive allegiance in the Shema with Jesus' affirmation of love for God and neighbor. In Mark 12, the scribe's response and the comparison with sacrifices further specify the force of the commands. The phrase's meaning is not exhausted by a physical-strength metaphor; its literary setting concerns covenant loyalty in thought and action.

The working synthesis interprets the sequence as a comprehensive summons rather than an inventory that divides the human being into competing parts. That reading should still preserve the individual words and the differences in their Greek reception. A theology review asks whether a proposal draws its account of worship and obedience from the dialogue rather than from a creatively expanded etymology. For retrieval, connect this entry to heart, nephesh, love, and listening as optional neighbors; use only the combination needed for the selected verse or question.

#### Extended Full word study: attested semantics, contextual controls and theological boundaries

### Full-depth semantic audit: meod as intensifier

Hebrew **מְאֹד (*me’od*)** most commonly acts as an adverb/intensifier: “very,” “greatly,” “exceedingly,” or the degree of an action or quality. Gen 1:31 describes creation as **very good**; here the word does not mean muscles or financial wealth. In Deut 6:5 the phrase **בְּכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ (*bekhol-me’odekha*)** follows heart and *nephesh* and expresses loving Yahweh with all one's “muchness” or full capacity/resources. Its possessive construction and series position produce the broader idiomatic effect; “strength” in English is an interpretation of the *whole phrase*, not the ordinary stand-alone lexical meaning of the adverb.

**Literary and reception context.** Deut 6:4–9 is a covenant appeal involving love, memory, teaching and loyalty; the audience is Israel and the object of love is Yahweh. Mark 12:29–30 cites the Shema in Greek with a list of heart, soul, mind and strength. Its several Greek nouns unpack the command's totalizing force; they do not establish that Hebrew *me’od* independently means all four faculties. Elsewhere the simple intensifier may modify a verb, adjective or quantity without becoming an anthropological technical term.

**Semantic limits.** Separate degree, amount, whole-capacity idiom, and later Greek reception. “Love with every resource” can communicate Deut 6:5 in explanatory paraphrase, provided the actual Hebrew wording and alternative “strength” tradition remain visible. A theology of wholehearted worship follows the literary unit rather than a universal muscular gloss for *me’od*. **Limit:** an exhaustive count of nominal and adverbial uses would need a complete concordance.
theology_check: Study the Shema and its NT reception as whole-person devotion without requiring identical lists of human faculties.
